Correct. With a route to the middle ear it risks cochlear damage and hearing loss, which makes an intact drum the thing to establish before prescribing it.
Ciprofloxacin
The fluoroquinolone drops are the ones considered safe in this situation.
Dexamethasone
The steroid component is not the part that carries this warning.
Ofloxacin
Ofloxacin is offered as an alternative rather than restricted.

D.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
D.q: By what mechanism do ocular glucocorticoids suppress the late-phase allergic reaction?
opts: They block cyclooxygenase only
That is the nonsteroidals, and it leaves the leukotriene arm untouched — which is precisely the difference.
They inhibit interleukin-2 production
Interleukin-2 inhibition is cyclosporine's mechanism in dry eye, and it works on T cells rather than on the arachidonic acid cascade.
They inhibit phospholipase A2
Correct. Cutting off arachidonic acid stops the whole downstream cascade, not just the prostaglandin arm. They also inhibit fibrin and collagen deposition, which is why they reduce scar formation.
They stabilize mast cell membranes
Mast cell stabilization acts earlier in the sequence, preventing mediator release rather than suppressing the cascade those mediators trigger.

D.io: Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: What limits ezetimibe's systemic exposure?
opts: Enterohepatic recirculation
Correct. Ezetimibe and its active glucuronide metabolite circulate enterohepatically, returning the drug to its site of action and limiting systemic exposure.
Extensive CYP3A4 metabolism
CYP3A4 metabolism is the story for atorvastatin, lovastatin and simvastatin. Ezetimibe's exposure is limited by enterohepatic recirculation.
Rapid renal excretion
Renal clearance is not the described reason. Enterohepatic recirculation keeps ezetimibe at its site of action.
It is not absorbed at all
Complete non-absorption describes bile acid sequestrants. Ezetimibe forms an active glucuronide and recirculates enterohepatically.

D.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Under the ACC/AHA (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association) guideline, why are lipids measured at follow-up visits?
opts: To titrate to an LDL goal
Titrating to an LDL target was the ATP III (Adult Treatment Panel III) approach that the newer guideline dropped.
To detect liver disease early
Follow-up lipid panels are not a liver screen; they are measured to assess adherence to treatment.
To decide whether to add niacin
The stated purpose of follow-up lipid measurement is to assess adherence to treatment.
To assess adherence
Correct. Lipids are measured at follow-up to assess adherence to treatment, not to reach a specific LDL (low-density lipoprotein) target.

D.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
D.q: Which adverse effect of the ocular nonsteroidals matters most in a patient already being watched for glaucoma?
opts: Reduced tear production
Increased lacrimation rather than reduced tearing is described, alongside keratitis and a rise in intraocular pressure.
Changes in eyelash length
That belongs to the prostaglandin analogs used in glaucoma, alongside iris color change.
Bradycardia
Slowing of the heart is a systemic effect of the topical beta blockers, reaching the circulation by the nasolacrimal route.
A rise in intraocular pressure
Correct. The drug given for inflammation pushes the very pressure the glaucoma treatment exists to lower, so the two work against each other.

D.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of antihypertensive drugs
D.q: When is thiocyanate toxicity most likely during nitroprusside therapy?
opts: The first minutes of infusion
Early toxicity is not thiocyanate. It accumulates with long infusions or in renal failure.
Long infusions or renal failure
Correct. Thiocyanate accumulates with long-term infusions or renal failure, causing weakness, anoxia, tinnitus, muscle spasms and toxic psychosis.
Only in slow acetylators
Acetylator status matters for hydralazine, not nitroprusside. Thiocyanate builds up with long infusions or renal failure.
Only after oral dosing
Nitroprusside is given by intravenous infusion. Thiocyanate toxicity follows long infusions or renal failure.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
D.q: How do beta blockers directly change myocardial oxygen supply?
opts: They dilate the coronary arteries
Coronary dilation is a nitrate effect (calcium channel blockers also dilate). Beta blockers leave oxygen supply unchanged and only lower demand.
They relieve coronary vasospasm
Relief of vasospasm belongs to calcium channel blockers and nitrates; beta blockers leave supply unchanged and only lower demand; they may worsen vasospastic angina.
They have no effect on supply
Correct. Beta blockers act on the demand side, lowering heart rate and contractility; they do not dilate the coronary arteries, so other antianginals are needed to raise supply.
They dilate areas of fixed stenosis
Mild dilation at fixed stenoses is a calcium channel blocker effect. Beta blockers do not change coronary flow; they lower demand.

D.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Cholestyramine reduces the absorption of which drug?
opts: Evolocumab
Evolocumab is injected, so a resin in the gut cannot affect its absorption. Warfarin, an oral drug, is on the list.
Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is given by intravenous infusion, bypassing the gut. Resins reduce absorption of oral drugs such as warfarin.
Esmolol
Esmolol is an intravenous beta blocker, so gut binding cannot affect it. Warfarin's absorption is reduced by resins.
Warfarin
Correct. As anion exchange resins they interfere with the absorption of digoxin, warfarin, thyroxine, beta blockers and thiazide diuretics.

D.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for antihypertensive drugs
D.q: A patient on enalapril has a bothersome dry cough but well-controlled blood pressure. Which change is most appropriate?
opts: Switch to a different ACE inhibitor
The cough is not related to the specific agent: every ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor lets bradykinin build up, so a switch within the class keeps the cough.
Halve the dose of enalapril
The cough is not dose-related, so halving the dose does not remove it. Moving to an angiotensin receptor blocker does.
Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Correct. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not affect bradykinin metabolism, so they do not cause cough, and they keep the benefit of blocking angiotensin II.
Add a beta blocker to suppress it
Beta blockers have no antitussive role and can cause bronchospasm. The fix is to change to a drug that spares bradykinin.

D.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
D.q: A patient with peripheral vascular disease starts a beta blocker. Which symptom may worsen?
opts: Leg pain with walking
Correct. Claudication is listed as a possible beta blocker adverse reaction, which is why peripheral vascular disease is a precaution.
Ankle swelling
Ankle swelling (peripheral edema) is typical of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; the beta blocker precaution in vascular disease is claudication.
Facial flushing
Flushing is an effect of nitrates and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; the beta blocker problem in vascular disease is claudication.
Constipation
Constipation is counseled with calcium channel blockers. The beta blocker precaution in peripheral vascular disease is claudication.

D.io: Identify ENT drug classes and commonly prescribed ENT drugs
D.q: Which agent is named as an over-the-counter sleep aid?
opts: Azelastine
Azelastine is a nasal spray for allergic and vasomotor rhinitis rather than a sleep aid; doxylamine is the sleep aid named.
Promethazine
Promethazine is named for its antimuscarinic and antiemetic strength.
Doxylamine
Correct. A sedating antihistamine sold for the side effect rather than the indication.
Fluticasone
Fluticasone is a nasal corticosteroid rather than an antihistamine. Doxylamine is the agent sold as a sleep aid.

D.io: Identify indications for commonly used drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Which patient falls into one of the four major statin benefit groups?
opts: A 35-year-old with diabetes and LDL of 120
The diabetes group covers ages 40 to 75 with LDL (low-density lipoprotein) 70 to 189 mg/dL; at 35 this patient falls outside it.
A 50-year-old with LDL of 150 and 3% risk
Without disease, diabetes or LDL above 190 mg/dL, a statin group needs a high estimated 10-year risk; 3% is low.
A 55-year-old after a myocardial infarction
Correct. Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is the first benefit group; the others are LDL above 190 mg/dL, diabetes at 40 to 75 with LDL 70 to 189, and high estimated risk.
A 60-year-old with diabetes and LDL of 60
The diabetes group requires LDL (low-density lipoprotein) of 70 to 189 mg/dL; 60 mg/dL falls below it.

D.io: Identify drug classes and commonly prescribed drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Which of these drugs is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
opts: Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe is the cholesterol absorption inhibitor, an oral drug acting at the brush border. The PCSK9 inhibitors are the -mab antibodies.
Evolocumab
Correct. Alirocumab and evolocumab are the PCSK9 inhibitors; the -mab suffix marks them as monoclonal antibodies.
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant. The PCSK9 inhibitors are alirocumab and evolocumab.
Fenofibrate
Fenofibrate is a fibrate that activates PPAR-alpha. Evolocumab is the PCSK9 inhibitor here.

D.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
D.q: Gentamicin and tobramycin act on the bacterial ribosome. At which subunit?
opts: The 50S subunit
That belongs to the macrolides — erythromycin and azithromycin — which block transpeptidation there.
Both the 30S and 50S subunits equally
Neither class does this; each has its own subunit and the separation is what makes the pair worth learning.
Neither — they act on the cell membrane
That is polymyxin B, which alters membrane permeability and lets intracellular contents leak out.
The 30S subunit
Correct. The aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit and interfere with protein synthesis. The macrolides take the 50S, and keeping the two numbers straight is the whole distinction.

D.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for myocardial ischemia drug therapy.
D.q: A 64-year-old man with known angina develops chest pressure at rest. He sits down and places one nitroglycerin tablet under his tongue. Five minutes later the pain is unchanged. What should he do next?
opts: Wait an hour to see if rest helps
Waiting delays care for what may be an infarction. The instruction is to call emergency services when the first dose has not relieved the pain.
Swallow a long-acting nitrate tablet
Long-acting nitrates are prophylactic adjuncts with a slow onset and are not rescue therapy for an attack that has not responded.
Take his beta blocker early
A beta blocker lowers demand over time and does not rescue an unrelieved attack. Emergency services are needed first.
Call emergency services
Correct. Chest pain unrelieved five minutes after the first nitroglycerin dose is treated as a possible acute coronary syndrome, so emergency help is called.

D.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: A patient starting niacin asks how to reduce the flushing. What is recommended?
opts: Take it with alcohol
Alcohol is listed as a niacin interaction and does not prevent flushing. Aspirin premedication does.
Take it with grapefruit juice
Grapefruit juice is a statin interaction and has no role in niacin flushing. Aspirin premedication minimizes it.
Take aspirin beforehand
Correct. Flushing is prostaglandin mediated and is minimized by premedication with aspirin.
Take it with an antacid
Antacids lower ezetimibe levels and do nothing for niacin flushing. Aspirin premedication minimizes it.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: How do fibrates raise HDL (high-density lipoprotein)?
opts: They block HDL breakdown in the gut
HDL is not broken down in the gut. Fibrates raise HDL by increasing ApoA-1 expression.
They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase
HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the statin mechanism. Fibrates raise HDL through increased ApoA-1 expression.
They bind cholesterol in the bile
Binding in the bile is not a fibrate action. Fibrates raise HDL by increasing ApoA-1 expression.
They increase ApoA-1 expression
Correct. PPAR-alpha activation increases expression of ApoA-1, the HDL apolipoprotein, raising HDL by 10 to 35%.

D.io: Identify contraindications for ENT drugs
D.q: Which allergy history is a contraindication to benzonatate?
opts: Allergy to penicillin or a cephalosporin
Unrelated to benzonatate. The relevant allergy is to tetracaine and related ester anesthetics.
Allergy to aspirin or other salicylates
Unrelated to benzonatate, which is chemically related to the ester local anesthetics such as tetracaine.
Allergy to iodine or contrast media
Unrelated to benzonatate. Allergy to tetracaine or a related anesthetic is the contraindication.
Allergy to tetracaine or related anesthetics
Correct. Benzonatate is chemically related to the ester local anesthetics, so a reaction to one predicts a reaction to the other.

D.io: Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of antihypertensive drugs
D.q: How do dihydropyridines differ from non-dihydropyridines with respect to CYP3A4?
opts: Substrates, not inhibitors
Correct. CYP3A4 inhibitors lengthen the half-life of both groups, but only the non-dihydropyridines inhibit CYP3A4 and alter other drugs through it.
Stronger CYP3A4 inhibitors
It is the non-dihydropyridines that inhibit CYP3A4. Dihydropyridines affect other drugs only pharmacodynamically.
Inducers of CYP3A4
Dihydropyridines are not described as inducers. They are substrates, so CYP3A4 inhibitors increase their half-life.
Unaffected by CYP3A4
They are affected: CYP3A4 inhibitors increase the dihydropyridine half-life. What they lack is the non-dihydropyridines' inhibitory effect.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Where does ezetimibe act?
opts: The terminal ileum
The terminal ileum is where resins block bile acid reabsorption. Ezetimibe acts at the intestinal brush border.
The intestinal brush border
Correct. Ezetimibe selectively inhibits cholesterol absorption at the brush border membrane, blocking sterol uptake in the upper small intestine.
The hepatocyte enzyme
Hepatocyte HMG-CoA reductase is the statin target. Ezetimibe acts in the intestine, at the brush border.
Adipose tissue
Reducing fatty acid mobilization from adipose tissue is niacin's action. Ezetimibe acts at the brush border.

D.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
D.q: A 68-year-old on a prostaglandin analog still has inadequate pressure control. What is the principle for adding a second agent?
opts: Add a second prostaglandin analog
Same mechanism gives no synergy.
Increase the prostaglandin to twice daily
That actively reduces its effect.
Add an agent with a DIFFERENT mechanism
Correct. Targeting a second route gives synergy, and fewer drops improves compliance. Which brand pairs which two drugs matters far less than the principle.
Add a topical steroid
Steroids raise intraocular pressure.

D.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: A patient on warfarin is started on gemfibrozil. Which interaction is expected?
opts: Reduced warfarin absorption
Reduced warfarin absorption is the bile acid sequestrant interaction, avoided by separating the doses. Fibrates increase warfarin's effect.
Reduced anticoagulant effect
The direction is the reverse: fibrates increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin.
Increased anticoagulant effect
Correct. Fibrates increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; they also interact with statins, ezetimibe and bile acid sequestrants.
No interaction is expected
There is a listed interaction: fibrates increase warfarin's anticoagulant effect.

D.io: Identify indications for commonly used antihypertensive drugs
D.q: Which drug is given by intravenous infusion for hypertensive crisis?
opts: Hydralazine
Hydralazine is listed for chronic hypertension with a diuretic and a beta blocker. Nitroprusside is the crisis infusion.
Nitroprusside
Correct. Nitroprusside is the hypertensive crisis agent, given by intravenous infusion; it dilates both veins and arterioles.
Minoxidil
Minoxidil is an oral agent for severe or refractory chronic hypertension. The crisis infusion is nitroprusside.
Clonidine
Clonidine is an oral central sympatholytic for chronic hypertension. Nitroprusside is given by infusion in a crisis.

D.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
D.q: A contact lens wearer has bacterial conjunctivitis and keratitis has been ruled out. Which class is preferred, and why?
opts: A macrolide, because erythromycin is soothing on an inflamed eye
True of erythromycin in general, and it is the commonest ophthalmic antibiotic — but soothing does not address the organism this patient is at risk from.
An aminoglycoside, because it covers gram-negative organisms
Aminoglycosides do have gram-negative activity, but the fluoroquinolones are the class named for Pseudomonas and corneal ulcers, and aminoglycosides carry a corneal ulceration risk of their own.
Sulfacetamide, because it is inexpensive and well tolerated
Cheap, but it does not answer the Pseudomonas risk, and it must be avoided altogether in sulfonamide allergy.
A fluoroquinolone, for Pseudomonas cover

Correct. Contact lens use raises the risk of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative rod, and the fluoroquinolones are the class that covers it. They are also the preferred choice for corneal ulcers for the same reason.

D.io: Identify contraindications for antihypertensive drugs
D.q: A patient with mild asthma needs a beta blocker after a myocardial infarction. Which choice carries the lowest risk of bronchospasm?
opts: Metoprolol
Correct. Bronchospasm is less likely with beta-1 selective agents such as metoprolol, because pulmonary beta-2 receptors are relatively spared.
Propranolol
Propranolol is non-selective and blocks pulmonary beta-2 receptors, the mechanism of bronchospasm in asthma.
Nadolol
Nadolol is non-selective, so it blocks the airway beta-2 receptors that keep bronchi relaxed. A beta-1 selective agent is safer.
Timolol
Timolol is non-selective; even as an eye drop its systemic beta-2 blockade can provoke bronchospasm. Metoprolol is beta-1 selective.

D.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for antihypertensive drugs
D.q: A patient with hypertension mildly above goal has a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 450 mg/g. Which initial therapy is recommended?
opts: A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
A dihydropyridine is a first-line option only when there is no albuminuria. At a ratio of 300 mg/g or more, the choice is an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.
A beta blocker or an alpha-1 blocker
Beta blockers are not first line, alpha-1 blockers are specialty add-ons, and neither offers kidney protection. Albuminuria of this degree calls for an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.
Hydralazine or minoxidil
Direct vasodilators are for severe or resistant hypertension with other agents. Albuminuria points to an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.
An ACE inhibitor or receptor blocker

Correct. With an albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 300 mg/g or more, the algorithm starts an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker, consistent with their kidney-protective effect.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: What mediates the cutaneous flushing caused by niacin?
opts: Prostaglandins
Correct. Niacin flushing is a prostaglandin-mediated effect, which is why premedication with aspirin minimizes it.
Bradykinin
Bradykinin accumulation causes the cough and angioedema of ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, not niacin flushing.
Histamine
Histamine is not the described mediator. Niacin flushing is prostaglandin mediated and blunted by aspirin.
Serotonin
Serotonin is not the described mediator. Niacin flushing is a prostaglandin-mediated effect.

D.io: Identify indications for commonly used ENT drugs
D.q: A patient using an inhaled steroid develops oral candidiasis. Which of these situations is NOT given as a setting for it?
opts: Use of an inhaled steroid
This is one of the named settings, along with HIV infection and chemotherapy, all of which share suppressed immunity.
Human immunodeficiency virus infection
This is one of the named settings, alongside inhaled steroid use and chemotherapy.
Chemotherapy
This is one of the named settings, alongside inhaled steroid use and HIV infection.
Recent tympanostomy tube placement
Correct -- this is not one of them. The settings given are inhaled steroids, HIV infection and chemotherapy, all of which share suppressed local or general immunity.

D.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ENT drugs
D.q: Histamine release produces the triple response. What are its three components?
opts: Redness, itching and sneezing
Itching and sneezing are symptoms rather than the components of the triple response.
Swelling, pallor and numbness
Pallor is the opposite of what histamine produces. The triple response is redness, a wheal and a surrounding flare.
Bronchospasm, hypotension and rash
That describes anaphylaxis rather than the local triple response.
Redness, a wheal, and a surrounding flare
Correct. Three visible signs from three different mechanisms -- direct vasodilation, leaking capillaries, and a nerve reflex -- which is why they appear together but look different.

D.io: Outline appropriate patient education for ENT drugs
D.q: What is a patient starting guaifenesin told to expect?
opts: Less drainage within a day
Increased drainage is what is expected, and saying so stops the patient reading the drug working as it failing.
A bitter taste
That belongs to the nasal sprays. A patient on guaifenesin is told to expect more drainage and to drink fluids.
More drainage
Correct. Warning the patient that drainage increases stops them reading the drug working as the drug failing. To drink plenty of fluid.
Drowsiness
Not an expected effect of guaifenesin. The patient is told to expect increased drainage and to drink plenty of fluid.

D.io: Identify ophthalmic drug classes and commonly prescribed ophthalmic drugs
D.q: Which three agents are listed as mast cell stabilizers?
opts: Olopatadine, epinastine and azelastine
All antihistamines, though several antihistamines do have some stabilizing activity.
Cromolyn, lodoxamide and nedocromil
Correct. A short list worth holding because everything else in the allergy section is an antihistamine, a vasoconstrictor or an anti-inflammatory.
Ketorolac, nepafenac and diclofenac
Ketorolac, nepafenac and diclofenac are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, which block cyclooxygenase rather than stabilizing mast cells.
Naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline and pheniramine
The first two are vasoconstrictors and the third an antihistamine found in combination products.

D.io: Identify indications for commonly used drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
D.q: Which class lowers LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol the most?
opts: Statins
Correct. Statins lower LDL by 18 to 55%, the most of any class; they are the most efficacious and first line.
Fibrates
Fibrates lower LDL only 5 to 20%; their strength is triglycerides and HDL (high-density lipoprotein).
Niacin
Niacin lowers LDL 5 to 25%; its strengths are raising HDL (high-density lipoprotein) and lowering triglycerides.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe lowers LDL about 18% and is used as an add-on to a statin.

D.io: Identify indications for commonly used ENT drugs
D.q: What are nasal corticosteroids indicated for?
opts: Acute bacterial sinusitis
Not their indication. Nasal corticosteroids are indicated for allergic and vasomotor rhinitis.
Allergic and vasomotor rhinitis
Correct. The same two conditions the nasal antihistamine covers, which is why the two are often used together.
Otitis externa
Not a nasal indication. Nasal corticosteroids treat allergic and vasomotor rhinitis.
Chronic cough
Not their stated indication, which is allergic and vasomotor rhinitis.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of antihypertensive drugs
D.q: How does clonidine lower blood pressure?
opts: Blocks central alpha-2 receptors
Clonidine activates rather than blocks these receptors; it is an alpha-2 agonist, and stimulation is what reduces sympathetic outflow.
Blocks vascular alpha-1 receptors
Peripheral alpha-1 blockade is the prazosin mechanism. Clonidine acts centrally by stimulating alpha-2 receptors.
Blocks renal beta-1 receptors
Blocking beta-1 receptors to reduce renin is a beta blocker action. Clonidine stimulates central alpha-2 receptors.
Stimulates central alpha-2 receptors
Correct. Clonidine is an alpha-2 and imidazoline agonist; stimulating central alpha-2A receptors inhibits sympathetic outflow and increases parasympathetic activity.

D.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with antihypertensive drugs
D.q: A patient with salt-sensitive hypertension responds poorly to losartan. What improves the response?
opts: Doubling the losartan dose
Receptors are saturated at starting doses, so dose increases change blood pressure only slightly. Adding a diuretic is what improves salt-sensitive hypertension.
Adding an ACE inhibitor
Pairing an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker is not the step; the recommended combinations add a diuretic or a dihydropyridine.
Adding a diuretic
Correct. Angiotensin receptor blockers are less effective in the salt-sensitive form; adding a diuretic improves outcomes, which is why most come as combination products.
Adding a potassium supplement
Potassium supplements raise the hyperkalemia risk with this class and do nothing for the salt-sensitive response. Adding a diuretic does.

E.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with ENT drugs
E.q: Why is ibuprofen a problem for a patient taking methotrexate?
opts: It displaces methotrexate from its receptor
Displacement at a receptor is not the described mechanism. Ibuprofen reduces methotrexate secretion, so it accumulates.
It prevents methotrexate from being absorbed
Absorption is not the step affected. Reduced secretion is what allows methotrexate to reach toxic levels.
It inactivates methotrexate in the liver
The interaction concerns secretion rather than hepatic inactivation.
It reduces methotrexate secretion
Correct. Same mechanism as the lithium interaction -- reduced renal clearance of a drug that does harm when it accumulates. Producing toxic levels.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia.
E.q: A 66-year-old man has chest pressure at rest and an electrocardiogram suggesting an acute coronary syndrome. He had an intracranial hemorrhage last week. Blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and heart rate is 80 beats per minute. Which of the following is contraindicated?
opts: Aspirin
Correct. Recent intracranial hemorrhage is a listed contraindication to aspirin, along with allergy and recent gastrointestinal bleeding.
Nitroglycerin
Its listed restrictions are hypotension and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, and a recent intracranial hemorrhage is not one of them.
Metoprolol
Its listed cautions are bradycardia, hypotension, heart block and severe reactive airway disease, and this patient has none of them.
Morphine
Its listed adverse effects are hypotension and allergy, and it does not impair clotting, so the hemorrhage is not the concern.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
E.q: Which second messenger do nitrates increase to relax vascular smooth muscle?
opts: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate is the messenger of beta receptor signaling, not the nitrate pathway, which raises cyclic guanosine monophosphate.
Cyclic guanosine monophosphate
Correct. Nitric oxide from nitrates stimulates conversion of guanosine triphosphate to cyclic guanosine monophosphate, which lowers calcium and relaxes smooth muscle.
Inositol trisphosphate
Inositol trisphosphate releases calcium and promotes contraction, the opposite of the nitrate effect, which runs through cyclic guanosine monophosphate.
Cytosolic calcium
Nitrates lower cytosolic calcium to relax smooth muscle; the messenger they raise is cyclic guanosine monophosphate.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: Which systemic adverse effects can a topical ophthalmic beta blocker produce?
opts: Hypertension and tachycardia
The opposite direction; beta blockade slows the heart rather than speeding it.
Central nervous system depression and apnea
That is the alpha-2 agonist risk, and specifically in children under two.
Bradycardia, heart block and bronchoconstriction
Correct. A drop is not a local-only treatment — nasolacrimal absorption avoids first-pass metabolism, so a topical beta blocker can do everything a systemic one does.
Bitter taste and allergic conjunctivitis
Bitter taste and allergic conjunctivitis are carbonic anhydrase inhibitor effects, and are local rather than systemic.

E.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ENT drugs
E.q: Otic preparations usually combine an anti-infective with a glucocorticoid. What does each component do?
opts: The steroid kills the organism and the anti-infective reduces swelling
The roles are the other way round: the anti-infective inhibits bacterial growth and the steroid reduces inflammatory cytokines.
Both components are antibacterial and act synergistically
The steroid has no antibacterial action. It is there to reduce inflammatory cytokines while the anti-infective inhibits bacterial growth.
The anti-infective inhibits bacterial growth and the steroid reduces inflammatory cytokines
Correct. Two separate jobs in one bottle, which is also why the combinations cost more than a plain antibiotic drop.
The steroid improves penetration of the anti-infective through the tympanic membrane
Penetration is not the stated reason for combining them. Each component has its own job: killing organisms, and damping inflammation.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used antihypertensive drugs
E.q: Clonidine has analgesic activity. What additional use does this support?
opts: Migraine prophylaxis
Migraine prophylaxis is an indication for propranolol, timolol and calcium channel blockers. Clonidine's extra use is blunting opiate withdrawal.
Prostatic hyperplasia
Benign prostatic hyperplasia is treated with alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin. Clonidine blunts opiate withdrawal reactions.
Essential tremor
Benign essential tremor responds to beta blockers through skeletal muscle beta-2 blockade. Clonidine's extra use is opiate withdrawal.
Blunting opiate withdrawal
Correct. Clonidine's analgesic activity blunts opiate withdrawal reactions.

E.io: Outline appropriate patient education for ENT drugs
E.q: Why is a patient who has taken a corticosteroid for more than about a week told not to stop abruptly?
opts: The drug accumulates and must be cleared slowly
Accumulation is not the reason given. Stopping abruptly after more than about a week produces rebound symptoms.
Stopping suddenly produces rebound symptoms
Correct. It is the duration that creates the problem, which is why a short course and a long one are stopped differently.
Abrupt withdrawal causes fluid retention
Fluid retention is an effect of taking the drug, not of stopping it.
The drug loses effect if restarted after a gap
Loss of future effect is not the concern. Abrupt withdrawal after a week or more produces rebound symptoms.

E.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: How do ocular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs reduce inflammation?
opts: They inhibit phospholipase A2, preventing arachidonic acid formation
That is the glucocorticoid mechanism, and the distinction between the two levels is the point.
They stabilize mast cells against degranulation
That is the antihistamines, which act on the receptor after histamine has been released rather than preventing its release.
They block cyclooxygenase
Correct. They act one step below the steroids: the steroids stop arachidonic acid being liberated at all, while the nonsteroidals stop what is already liberated becoming prostaglandin.
They inactivate the H1 receptor
That is the antihistamines, which are inverse agonists at the H1 receptor rather than agents that prevent mediator release.

E.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: A patient has taken cholestyramine for years. Which deficiency is she at risk of?
opts: Potassium, magnesium and zinc
Electrolyte loss of this kind is not a listed resin effect. They cause malabsorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and folic acid.
Fat-soluble vitamins and folate
Correct. Resins cause malabsorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and of folic acid.
Water-soluble B vitamins and iron
Iron and the water-soluble B vitamins are not the listed deficiencies. Resins impair absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K and folic acid.
Sodium, chloride and bicarbonate
Sodium, chloride and bicarbonate loss is not described. The malabsorption is of vitamins A, D, E and K and folic acid.

E.io: Identify contraindications for antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A patient with hypertension also has heart failure. Which calcium channel blocker avoids the relative contraindication in heart failure?
opts: Verapamil
Verapamil has the strongest suppression of contractility and can exacerbate heart failure; heart failure is a relative contraindication to it.
Amlodipine

Correct. Heart failure is a relative contraindication to the non-dihydropyridines because they suppress contractility; amlodipine, a dihydropyridine approved for hypertension, has little effect on contractility.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine; heart failure is a relative contraindication because of its negative inotropic effect.
Nimodipine
Nimodipine is a dihydropyridine, but its approved indication is subarachnoid hemorrhage, not hypertension. Amlodipine is the hypertension choice.

E.io: Describe adverse effects of antihypertensive drugs
E.q: Which pair of side effects is typical of central sympatholytics?
opts: Cough and angioedema
Cough and angioedema are bradykinin effects of ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, not central sympatholytics.
Flushing and tachycardia
Flushing with reflex tachycardia belongs to vasodilators such as dihydropyridines and hydralazine. Central agents cause sedation and dry mouth.
Hair growth and edema
Hypertrichosis with fluid retention points to minoxidil. The central sympatholytic pair is sedation and dry mouth.
Sedation and dry mouth
Correct. Drowsiness or sedation and dry mouth are central effects; sexual dysfunction, a narrow therapeutic range and abrupt withdrawal hypertension complete the list.

E.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
E.q: A 19-year-old contact lens wearer has purulent conjunctivitis. Keratitis has been excluded. Which class do you reach for, and why?
opts: A macrolide, because it is soothing on the inflamed eye
Erythromycin is soothing and cheap, but it does not cover the organism this patient is at risk from.
A fluoroquinolone
Correct, and the same class is preferred for corneal ulcers for the same reason. Because lens wearers are at high risk for Pseudomonas.
An aminoglycoside, because it covers gram negatives
Its risk of corneal ulceration makes it a poor choice in an eye already at risk.
Sulfacetamide, because it is inexpensive
Cost is not the deciding factor when Pseudomonas is the concern.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia.
E.q: A 24-year-old college athlete has exertional chest pain and near-syncope. A systolic murmur grows louder with the Valsalva maneuver, and echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with outflow obstruction. Which drug class would be harmful?
opts: A beta blocker
Obstructive cardiomyopathy is not among the listed contraindications for a beta blocker; the nitrates are the class to avoid.
A non-dihydropyridine
Obstructive cardiomyopathy is not among the listed contraindications for these agents. The nitrates are the class contraindicated here.
A nitrate
Correct. Obstructive cardiomyopathy is a listed nitrate contraindication, and aortic stenosis is the other structural one.
An antiplatelet drug
It does not change ventricular filling or outflow, so the obstruction does not forbid it; the vasodilating nitrates are the concern.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: Which adverse effect is specific enough to an ophthalmic antibiotic class to be worth knowing, rather than being shared by all of them?
opts: Ocular irritation with erythromycin
Shared by nearly every ophthalmic antibiotic, which is why it is not worth memorizing which ones cause it.
Corneal ulceration from an aminoglycoside

Correct. Ocular irritation is common to essentially every agent here and so distinguishes nothing — but aminoglycosides used for several days can produce corneal ulceration and a reactive keratoconjunctivitis, which changes how long you continue them.
Hypersensitivity with bacitracin
Also non-specific — any of these agents can produce hypersensitivity, so it names no particular drug.
Unpleasant taste after a macrolide
The taste complaint belongs with the fluoroquinolones, and reflects nasolacrimal drainage rather than a class toxicity.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: In which patient is a statin contraindicated?
opts: A patient aged 50 with diabetes
Diabetes at ages 40 to 75 with LDL (low-density lipoprotein) 70 to 189 mg/dL is a statin benefit group, not a contraindication.
A patient after a heart attack
Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is the first statin benefit group, not a contraindication.
A patient who is pregnant
Correct. Hepatic disease and pregnancy are the statin contraindications.
A patient with LDL of 210 mg/dL
LDL (low-density lipoprotein) above 190 mg/dL is a statin benefit group. Pregnancy is the contraindication here.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: Which classes INCREASE aqueous outflow?
opts: Prostaglandins, alpha adrenergic agonists and cholinergic agonists
Correct. The alpha agonists appear on both sides — they decrease production and increase outflow — which is why they are easy to misplace.
Beta blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and prostaglandins
The first two decrease production; only the prostaglandins in this list increase outflow.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and cholinergic agonists only
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce production rather than improving drainage.
Beta blockers alone
Beta blockers are a production drug, and second line at that.

E.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which lifestyle measure raises HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol?
opts: Grapefruit juice
Grapefruit juice is a CYP-mediated statin interaction, not a way to raise HDL. Exercise raises HDL.
Exercise
Correct. HDL increases with exercise, a lifestyle measure that complements the drug classes that raise it, niacin and fibrates.
Salt substitutes
Salt substitutes add potassium and matter with ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors. Exercise raises HDL.
Fasting before meals
Fasting before meals is not a listed way to raise HDL; exercise is the lifestyle measure that raises it.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: How does the technique for a gel or ointment differ from a drop?
opts: The lacrimal duct must be covered for twice as long
The opposite is true: ointment does not drain like a solution, so the punctal occlusion step is unnecessary rather than prolonged.
The eye should be held open rather than closed
The eye is closed as with a drop; the difference is the duct step.
It should be applied directly to the cornea rather than the pocket
Medication goes into the lower lid pocket either way; nothing is applied to the cornea directly.
A ribbon into the pocket, with no duct occlusion
Correct. The process is otherwise the same, but ointment does not drain away like a solution, so the punctal occlusion step is unnecessary.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: How long may an over-the-counter ocular vasoconstrictor be used, and what should the patient be told if there is no improvement?
opts: Under two weeks; see a provider if no better in 72 hours
Correct. Short-term use only, because of rebound hyperemia. And the 72-hour rule exists because a red eye that is not improving may be something more serious than allergy.
Up to three months, with review if symptoms persist
Far too long — prolonged use is exactly what produces the rebound.
Indefinitely, as they are available without prescription
Being over the counter says nothing about safe duration; this is the misconception the counseling point exists to correct.
Less than two weeks, but no review is needed if symptoms persist
The duration is right and the advice is wrong: failure to improve in 72 hours is a reason to be seen.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to niacin?
opts: Peptic ulcer disease
Peptic ulcer disease is a relative, not absolute, contraindication to niacin. Chronic liver disease is absolute.
History of symptomatic gout
Symptomatic gout is a relative contraindication, because niacin raises uric acid. Chronic liver disease is absolute.
Diabetes with glucose intolerance
Diabetes is a relative contraindication, since niacin decreases glucose tolerance. Chronic liver disease is absolute.
Chronic liver disease
Correct. Chronic liver disease is the absolute contraindication; peptic ulcer disease, symptomatic gout, significant hyperuricemia and diabetes are relative ones.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used antihypertensive drugs
E.q: For hypertension, which patient is a beta blocker expected to work best in?
opts: A young patient with resting tachycardia
Correct. They work best in young patients with resting tachycardia, raised catecholamines and raised renin, though fatigue and limited exercise are common complaints.
An older patient with asthma
Asthma is where beta blockers cause bronchospasm. The group they work best in is young patients with resting tachycardia and high renin.
A patient with intermittent claudication
Claudication worsens with beta-2 blockade of vessels. Beta blockers work best in young patients with resting tachycardia.
A patient with frequent hypoglycemia
Beta blockers prolong hypoglycemia and mask its warning signs. They work best in young patients with resting tachycardia.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used ENT drugs
E.q: A patient on an inhaled steroid has oral thrush and takes several other medicines. Which antifungal is preferred, and why?
opts: Ketoconazole, because it is the more potent agent
Ketoconazole is absorbed and inhibits CYP3A4, which is the problem in a patient on several medicines.
Either one, since neither is absorbed at all
Ketoconazole is absorbed; nystatin is the nonabsorbable one.
Neither, since thrush resolves without treatment
Oral candidiasis is a stated indication for treatment, and nystatin treats it without reaching the rest of the patient.
Nystatin, because it is not absorbed

Correct. The property that limits it to surface infection is the same one that keeps it out of the patient's other drugs. Not being absorbed is also why it cannot interact with the patient's other medicines.

E.io: Identify drug classes and commonly prescribed drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which of these statins is one of the two that can reach high intensity?
opts: Atorvastatin
Correct. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are the only statins that reach high intensity (50% or greater lowering of LDL, low-density lipoprotein, cholesterol).
Simvastatin
Simvastatin reaches moderate or low intensity only. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are the high-intensity statins.
Pitavastatin
Pitavastatin is listed only as moderate intensity. The two high-intensity statins are atorvastatin and rosuvastatin.
Pravastatin
Pravastatin is moderate or low intensity. Only atorvastatin and rosuvastatin reach high intensity.

E.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of ENT drugs
E.q: Which illnesses typically precede Reye's syndrome?
opts: Bacterial otitis media or sinusitis
The preceding illnesses described are viral: an upper respiratory infection, influenza or chickenpox.
Streptococcal pharyngitis
Not among the illnesses named. Reye's syndrome follows an upper respiratory infection, influenza or chickenpox.
Gastroenteritis from food poisoning
Not among the illnesses named; the preceding illnesses are viral ones such as influenza and chickenpox.
An upper respiratory infection
Correct. All viral, which is why the aspirin restriction in children is framed around fever from viral illness specifically. Influenza or chickenpox.

E.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: Bacitracin ointment works on a structure none of the other ophthalmic antibiotics target. Which one?
opts: The 50S ribosomal subunit
That is the macrolides, which block transpeptidation there and stop protein synthesis.
The bacterial cell wall
Correct. Bacitracin stops mucopeptides being transferred into the growing wall. Every other ophthalmic antibiotic goes after the ribosome, DNA, folate or the membrane.
DNA gyrase
That is the fluoroquinolones, which cause double-stranded DNA breakage.
The cytoplasmic membrane
That is polymyxin B, which alters permeability rather than blocking wall construction.

E.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A patient on lisinopril begins taking ibuprofen daily for knee pain. How do NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) affect the ACE inhibitor?
opts: They increase its effect
The direction is wrong. NSAIDs blunt the drug, because they block prostaglandin-driven relaxation that bradykinin produces.
They reduce its effect
Correct. NSAIDs block the prostaglandin-dependent, bradykinin-mediated relaxation that contributes to the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor's effect, so blood pressure control weakens.
They have no interaction
There is a listed interaction: NSAIDs decrease the effect of ACE inhibitors by blocking bradykinin-mediated relaxation that depends on prostaglandins.
They cause its cough
The cough comes from bradykinin and substance P accumulating in the lungs, not from NSAIDs; NSAIDs instead reduce the drug's effect.

E.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
E.q: A 74-year-old on timolol drops for glaucoma develops systemic side effects. By what route did the drug reach the circulation?
opts: Nasolacrimal drainage
Correct. What runs down the duct is absorbed systemically without passing through the liver first. Which also avoids first-pass metabolism.
Transcorneal absorption into the bloodstream
Transcorneal absorption is what produces the LOCAL ocular effect.
Absorption through the eyelid skin
Eyelid skin is not the described route. It is the nasolacrimal duct.
Swallowed residue from the eyelashes
Swallowed residue is not the described mechanism; drainage down the nasolacrimal duct is.

E.io: Identify contraindications for antihypertensive drugs
E.q: Which statement about ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors in pregnancy is accurate?
opts: Contraindicated in the second and third trimesters
Correct. They cause fetal morbidity and mortality, including birth defects and fetal death, so they are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters.
Safe once the first trimester has ended
The danger is greatest after the first trimester: they are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of birth defects and fetal death.
Contraindicated in the first trimester only
The trimesters named are the second and third, when fetal morbidity and mortality occur, not the first alone.
Preferred for hypertension throughout pregnancy
They cause birth defects and fetal death and are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters, so they are never the preferred pregnancy agent.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: When resins deplete the bile acid pool, which hepatic enzyme increases to convert cholesterol into bile acids?
opts: Acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase
Acyl-coenzyme A:cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol for storage and packaging; it does not convert cholesterol into bile acids.
Lipoprotein lipase in plasma
Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes triglyceride in chylomicrons and very low-density lipoprotein; it does not make bile acids. Cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase does.
Cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase
Correct. Increased 7-alpha hydroxylase activity converts more cholesterol to bile acids, and the liver adds LDL receptors, increasing VLDL and LDL removal.
Hepatic HMG-CoA reductase
HMG-CoA reductase is the statin target in cholesterol synthesis; it does not convert cholesterol into bile acids. Cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase does.

E.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: Which cells are the principal targets in ocular hypersensitivity, and what happens when immunoglobulin E binds them?
opts: Neutrophils and macrophages; binding triggers phagocytosis
Neutrophils and macrophages are not the principal target cells named; immunoglobulin E binds Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils.
T lymphocytes; binding triggers interleukin-2 release
Interleukin-2 and T cells are where cyclosporine acts in dry eye, not the immediate allergic response.
Corneal epithelial cells; binding triggers prostaglandin release
The principal target cells named are mast cells and basophils.
Mast cells and basophils, within seconds

Correct. Immunoglobulin E binds Fc receptors, tyrosine kinases activate within 5 to 15 seconds, and histamine, platelet-activating factor and leukotrienes are released — producing vasodilation, swelling, redness and itch.

E.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A patient on diltiazem is started on amiodarone. What pharmacodynamic risk does the combination carry?
opts: Excess slowing of the heart
Correct. Amiodarone with a non-dihydropyridine can slow the sinus rate or worsen atrioventricular block; digoxin and beta blockers are listed alongside it.
Reflex tachycardia
Reflex tachycardia comes from dihydropyridine vasodilation. Amiodarone added to diltiazem slows the heart further rather than speeding it.
Hyperkalemia
Potassium is not the concern of this pair. The risk is additive nodal suppression: a slower sinus rate or worsened atrioventricular block.
Loss of diltiazem effect
The effects add rather than cancel. The combination slows the sinus rate or worsens atrioventricular block.

E.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
E.q: Which risk factor for coronary heart disease can a patient change?
opts: Age older than 45 in men
Age is fixed. Male age over 45 and female age over 55 are non-modifiable risk factors.
Age older than 55 in women
Age cannot be changed. Female age over 55 is a non-modifiable risk factor, unlike tobacco use, which can be stopped.
Tobacco use
Correct. Tobacco use, a sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, overweight, hypertension and dyslipidemia are modifiable risk factors that therapy targets.
Family history of premature events
A family history of a premature cardiovascular event is non-modifiable, unlike tobacco use, diabetes or hypertension.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: What distinguishes angle closure glaucoma from open angle glaucoma?
opts: Increased aqueous production with a gradual course
Increased production or reduced drainage with a gradual course describes open angle disease, not the mechanical blockage of angle closure.
Blockage of the drainage canal, with acute pain

Correct. Open angle comes from increased production or reduced drainage and damages the nerve over time; angle closure is a mechanical blockage that presents acutely and painfully. Drug therapy targets open angle disease.
Optic nerve damage at a normal intraocular pressure
Optic nerve damage at a normal pressure would be normal tension disease. Angle closure is defined by the blocked drainage canal.
Raised pressure without any optic nerve damage
Raised pressure with no optic nerve damage is ocular hypertension — a risk factor rather than either form of glaucoma.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which two classes both lower triglycerides by 20 to 50% and raise HDL (high-density lipoprotein) substantially?
opts: Resins and ezetimibe
Resins can raise triglycerides and ezetimibe barely affects HDL. Fibrates and niacin share this profile.
Fibrates and niacin
Correct. Both lower triglycerides by 20 to 50% and raise HDL (niacin 15 to 35%, fibrates 10 to 35%).
Statins and resins
Statins and resins are chiefly LDL (low-density lipoprotein) lowering agents, and resins can raise triglycerides.
Ezetimibe and statins
These lower LDL (low-density lipoprotein) through the supply and synthesis sides. Fibrates and niacin lower triglycerides and raise HDL.

E.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A 64-year-old with chronic kidney disease who uses a salt substitute is started on lisinopril. Which laboratory abnormality is most important to anticipate?
opts: Hypokalemia
The direction is wrong: less aldosterone means potassium is retained, so potassium rises rather than falls, especially with kidney disease and a salt substitute.
Hypercalcemia
Calcium is not the concern with ACE inhibitors. Renal disease plus a potassium-containing salt substitute makes hyperkalemia the one to watch.
Hypoglycemia
Masked or prolonged hypoglycemia is a beta blocker problem. With an ACE inhibitor, renal disease and a salt substitute, potassium rises.
Hyperkalemia
Correct. Hyperkalemia is most often seen with renal disease and in those taking potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes; this patient has two of those.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Where in the gut do resins block the reabsorption of bile acids?
opts: The stomach
Bile acids are not reabsorbed in the stomach. Resins act at the terminal ileum, where enterohepatic reabsorption occurs.
The brush border of the jejunum
Brush-border sterol uptake in the upper small intestine is where ezetimibe acts. Resins block bile acid reabsorption at the terminal ileum.
The gallbladder wall
The gallbladder stores and secretes bile; it is not the reabsorption site. Resins block bile acid reabsorption at the terminal ileum.
The terminal ileum
Correct. Bile acids are normally reabsorbed at the terminal ileum and recirculated to the liver; resins block that reabsorption so bile acid excretion rises.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of antihypertensive drugs
E.q: Why are arterial vessels 3 to 10 times more sensitive to calcium channel blockers than myocardial cells?
opts: Myocytes lack L-type calcium channels
Myocytes do have L-type channels; they supply the trigger calcium. The difference is that myocytes also recycle calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Arteries store more internal calcium
It is the reverse: myocytes have the recirculating internal store, while arteries depend on calcium entering through L-type channels.
Arteries rely on outside calcium entry
Correct. Arterial smooth muscle depends on exogenous calcium through L-type channels, whereas myocytes also draw on a recirculating store in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Arteries carry more beta-2 receptors
Beta receptors are not how calcium channel blockers act. The sensitivity comes from arteries depending on calcium entry through L-type channels.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of antihypertensive drugs
E.q: How does minoxidil relax arteriolar smooth muscle?
opts: Raises nitric oxide and cyclic GMP
Nitric oxide activating cyclic GMP is nitroprusside's mechanism (and a proposed one for hydralazine). Minoxidil opens potassium channels.
Opens ATP-modulated potassium channels
Correct. Increased potassium efflux hyperpolarizes the cell and relaxes the muscle; its action on potassium channels also causes arrhythmias.
Blocks L-type calcium channels
L-type calcium channel blockade is the calcium channel blocker mechanism. Minoxidil hyperpolarizes cells by opening potassium channels.
Blocks vascular alpha-1 receptors
Alpha-1 blockade is prazosin's mechanism. Minoxidil opens ATP-modulated potassium channels.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used ENT drugs
E.q: A child with acute otitis media finished a course of antibiotics three weeks ago. How does that change the choice?
opts: The same high-dose amoxicillin is used
Recent exposure is one of the stated reasons to move off plain amoxicillin.
A macrolide is substituted
Macrolides are a penicillin-allergy option, and pneumococcal resistance to them is common.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is used instead
Correct. Recent antibiotic exposure selects for beta-lactamase producers, and that is exactly what the clavulanate is there to cover.
Antibiotics are withheld for a further week
Watchful waiting is not the response to recent antibiotic exposure.

E.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which laboratory change occurs when ezetimibe is combined with a statin?
opts: Raised hepatic transaminases
Correct. Ezetimibe's adverse effects are gastrointestinal effects and elevated hepatic transaminases when combined with statins.
Raised serum potassium
Raised potassium belongs to ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, not ezetimibe.
Raised serum uric acid
Raised uric acid is a niacin effect at larger doses. Ezetimibe with a statin raises hepatic transaminases.
Raised serum calcium
Calcium is not affected by ezetimibe. The listed laboratory change with a statin is raised hepatic transaminases.

E.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which lipid-lowering class can RAISE triglycerides?
opts: Fibric acid derivatives
Fibrates lower triglycerides by 20 to 50%; they are the treatment for very high levels.
Bile acid sequestrants
Correct. Resins show no change or a rise in triglycerides, because they may increase VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) production.
Nicotinic acid (niacin)
Niacin lowers triglycerides by 20 to 50% and raises HDL (high-density lipoprotein) the most of any class.
HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors
Statins lower triglycerides modestly, by about 7 to 30%. Resins are the class that can raise them.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia.
E.q: A 52-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and ST-segment elevation. Blood pressure differs between the two arms, and imaging shows an aortic dissection. Which drug is contraindicated?
opts: Metoprolol
A beta blocker lowers heart rate and shear stress on the aortic wall, and dissection does not forbid it.
Labetalol
It blocks alpha and beta receptors to lower pressure and heart rate and is used in dissection.
Morphine
It is an analgesic and aortic dissection does not forbid it.
Tenecteplase
Correct. Aortic dissection is a contraindication to fibrinolysis, because clot lysis can lead to catastrophic bleeding.

E.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of ENT drugs
E.q: A patient on a first generation antihistamine reports dry mouth, blurred vision and difficulty passing urine. What explains this?
opts: The antimuscarinic action of the drug
Correct. Three complaints from three different organs, all explained by one receptor family being blocked.
Histamine receptor blockade itself
These effects come from the muscarinic blockade rather than the H1 blockade.
An allergic reaction to the drug
This is a predictable pharmacological effect rather than an allergy.
Interaction with alcohol
Alcohol adds sedation rather than these effects. Dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention are antimuscarinic.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary fat away from the intestine?
opts: Chylomicrons
Correct. Chylomicrons are secreted by intestinal cells; lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes their triglyceride core, and the liver removes the remnants.
Very low-density lipoprotein
Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) is made by the liver from carbohydrate and fatty acids, carrying endogenous rather than dietary fat.
Low-density lipoprotein
Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is the product of VLDL and IDL breakdown in plasma, not the carrier of dietary fat from the gut.
High-density lipoprotein
High-density lipoprotein (HDL) transfers cholesteryl ester to other particles and returns cholesterol to the liver; chylomicrons carry dietary fat.

E.io: Outline appropriate patient education for antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A 72-year-old starting verapamil asks which change in bowel habit to watch for. What should she be told?
opts: Constipation
Correct. Constipation is among the listed gastrointestinal effects of non-dihydropyridines, so bowel habits are worth asking about at follow-up.
Black stools
Stools that may turn black are listed for hydralazine, not verapamil. Verapamil's bowel effect to warn about is constipation.
Oily, fatty stools
Fatty stools are not a verapamil effect; the listed gastrointestinal problem to watch for is constipation.
Bloody diarrhea
Bloody diarrhea is not a listed effect. The non-dihydropyridine bowel effect patients should know about is constipation.

E.io: Identify antihypertensive drug classes and commonly prescribed antihypertensive drugs
E.q: A patient's medication list includes ramipril. To which drug class does it belong?
opts: Angiotensin receptor blockers
Angiotensin receptor blockers end in -sartan (losartan, valsartan). A -pril ending identifies an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor instead.
Dihydropyridine blockers
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers end in -dipine (amlodipine, nifedipine). Ramipril's -pril ending marks an ACE inhibitor.
ACE inhibitors
Correct. The -pril suffix marks an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor; ramipril sits alongside lisinopril, enalapril, benazepril and quinapril.
Beta blockers
Beta blockers end in -lol (metoprolol, atenolol). The -pril suffix belongs to the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used ENT drugs
E.q: What is N-acetylcysteine traditionally used for, apart from its mucolytic action?
opts: Acetaminophen poisoning
Correct. The same drug turns up in two entirely unrelated places -- as an antidote in poisoning and as a mucolytic in the airway -- which is worth noticing rather than being surprised by.
Aspirin poisoning
Not its antidotal use. N-acetylcysteine is traditionally the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning.
Opioid overdose
Not its antidotal use; N-acetylcysteine is the traditional antidote in acetaminophen poisoning.
Organophosphate poisoning
Not its antidotal use. Its established role outside the airway is in acetaminophen poisoning.

E.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with ENT drugs
E.q: What should a patient who drinks alcohol regularly be told about acetaminophen?
opts: The combination risks liver damage over time
Correct. Neither is dangerous on its own at ordinary use, which is what makes the combination easy to arrive at without noticing.
Alcohol prevents acetaminophen from working
Efficacy is not the concern; hepatic injury is. Regular alcohol with acetaminophen raises the risk of liver damage over time.
The combination causes gastric ulceration
Ulceration belongs to the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
There is no interaction between the two drugs
A chronic interaction is described, and it involves the liver.

E.io: Identify contraindications for ENT drugs
E.q: Which patients should avoid ibuprofen?
opts: Those with a history of Reye's syndrome
Reye's relates to aspirin in children rather than to ibuprofen.
Those taking acetaminophen
Acetaminophen is not a contraindication to ibuprofen. The contraindications are asthma, prior ulcer or perforation, and renal impairment.
Those over sixty-five years old
Age alone is not the stated contraindication; asthma, previous ulceration and renal impairment are, along with very young infants.
Those with asthma it may worsen
Correct. Asthma is the one most easily forgotten, because it is not an obvious consequence of blocking prostaglandin synthesis. Previous ulcer or perforation, or renal impairment.

E.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of ENT drugs
E.q: Which complications of persistent coughing are described as common?
opts: Stroke, syncope and rib fracture
These are described as the less common complications. The common ones are insomnia, exhaustion, musculoskeletal pain and hoarseness.
Pneumothorax, hemoptysis and chest pain
Not among the complications listed. The common ones are insomnia, exhaustion, musculoskeletal pain and hoarseness.
Insomnia, exhaustion, pain and hoarseness
Correct. Unglamorous but genuinely disabling, and together they are the reason cough is treated at all. The pain is musculoskeletal, from the effort of coughing.
Hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo
Not among the complications listed; insomnia, exhaustion, musculoskeletal pain and hoarseness are the common ones.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: What is the stated goal of treating infectious conjunctivitis?
opts: Relieve symptoms while the infection resolves on its own
That is the approach to adenoviral conjunctivitis specifically, where no antiviral exists.
Prevent transmission to the other eye
Limiting spread matters practically, but the goal given is to eradicate the infection and prevent the long-term complications it would leave.
Eradicate the infection and prevent long-term complications
Correct. Both halves matter — clearing the organism is not the whole aim, because the reason to treat promptly is what an untreated infection leaves behind.
Establish the organism by culture
Cultures are not routine unless an unusual organism is expected.

E.io: Identify indications for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
E.q: Why are nitrates used in acute coronary syndrome?
opts: To relieve chest pain
Correct. Nitrates give relief of chest pain only; they show no mortality benefit and no improvement in outcomes.
To lower mortality
Nitrates have no mortality benefit. Aspirin lowers mortality, while nitrates only relieve chest pain.
To limit infarct size
Reduced infarct size is a beta blocker benefit. Nitrates provide relief of chest pain without improving outcomes.
To prevent reinfarction
Reinfarction is reduced by aspirin. Nitrates are used for chest pain relief and do not improve outcomes.

E.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
E.q: A 35-year-old with predictable seasonal allergy cannot tolerate antihistamine drops and is willing to start weeks before the season. Which class suits her?
opts: An ophthalmic antibiotic
There is no infection to treat.
A vasoconstrictor used daily through the season
Prolonged use causes rebound hyperemia.
A mast cell stabilizer
Correct. Slow to work — 5 to 14 days — but that matters less when treatment starts before the season.
A topical glucocorticoid through the season
Steroids are limited to pulses of under two weeks.

E.io: Identify indications for drugs used to treat myocardial ischemia
E.q: Which drug manages chest pain that does not respond to nitrates in ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: Metoprolol
Metoprolol lowers infarct size and sudden cardiac death but is not the analgesic for pain unresponsive to nitrates. Morphine is used for that.
Aspirin
Aspirin reduces mortality and reinfarction, not pain. Morphine is the opioid analgesic used for pain unresponsive to nitrates.
Alteplase
Alteplase is a fibrinolytic that restores flow in ST-elevation infarction; it is not an analgesic. Morphine manages nitrate-resistant pain.
Morphine
Correct. Morphine, an opioid analgesic, is used for chest pain unresponsive to nitrates in ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

E.io: Describe adverse effects of antihypertensive drugs
E.q: Which effect on blood lipids has been reported with prazosin?
opts: A rise in triglycerides
Raised triglycerides are listed as a beta blocker adverse effect. Prazosin mildly lowers triglycerides and LDL (low-density lipoprotein).
A rise in LDL
Prazosin is reported to mildly reduce LDL (low-density lipoprotein), not raise it, while increasing HDL (high-density lipoprotein).
A mild rise in HDL
Correct. Prazosin shows evidence of a mild reduction in LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and triglycerides and increased HDL (high-density lipoprotein).
A large fall in HDL
The reported change is a mild increase in HDL (high-density lipoprotein), not a fall.

E.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of ENT drugs
E.q: How is acetaminophen tolerated when taken as intended?
opts: Poorly, with frequent gastric irritation
Gastric irritation belongs to the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Very well, with no notable side effects
Correct. Its safety within the intended range is exactly why exceeding that range is so easy to do. That holds at therapeutic exposure, which is what makes exceeding it so easy.
With common renal impairment
Renal effects belong to the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
With frequent sedation
Sedation is not an acetaminophen effect. Within the intended range it is described as very well tolerated.

E.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ENT drugs
E.q: H1 and H2 receptors both cause vasodilation. How do the two differ?
opts: H1 is slow and sustained, H2 is rapid and brief
The timings are the other way round: H1 vasodilation is rapid and short-lived, H2 is slow in onset and long-lasting.
H1 is rapid in onset and short-lived
Correct. Same end result by two different routes and on two different timescales, which is why blocking H1 alone does not abolish the flush. H2 is slow in onset and long-lasting.
Both are rapid and brief
They differ in timing, which is the point of comparing them.
Only H1 causes vasodilation
H2 causes vasodilation as well, by a slower and longer-lasting route, which is why blocking H1 alone does not abolish flushing.

E.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
E.q: What are the main uses of ocular glucocorticoids?
opts: First-line treatment of all allergic conjunctivitis
Antihistamines come first; steroids are for severe or refractory disease.
Bacterial keratitis, to limit scarring
Steroids suppress local immunity and appear on the fungal keratitis risk list; they are not a treatment for active infection.
Chronic dry eye as maintenance therapy
Cyclosporine holds that role; steroids cannot be used long term.
Severe allergy, uveitis and post-surgical inflammation
Correct. They are generally reserved for refractory symptoms, and can be given topically or intraocularly depending on the indication.

E.io: Identify indications for commonly used drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: What is the primary indication for a fibrate?
opts: LDL over 190 in a young adult
LDL (low-density lipoprotein) above 190 mg/dL is a statin benefit group. Fibrates are for very high triglycerides or low HDL.
High LDL during pregnancy
Pregnancy contraindicates fibrates; resins are the class approved in pregnancy.
Statin-induced raised enzymes
Rising liver enzymes on a statin are managed by lowering the dose or pausing it, not with a fibrate, whose own indication is very high triglycerides or low HDL.
Triglycerides over 1000 or low HDL
Correct. The primary indication is triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL or low HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol.

E.io: Identify contraindications for drugs that lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels
E.q: A patient with high triglycerides has a history of symptomatic gout. Which triglyceride-lowering option is best avoided?
opts: Fenofibrate
Gout is not a fibrate contraindication; fenofibrate lowers triglycerides without raising uric acid.
Gemfibrozil
Gemfibrozil is a fibrate; its contraindications are pregnancy, severe hepatic or renal dysfunction and gallbladder disease, not gout.
Niacin
Correct. Niacin raises uric acid, so symptomatic gout and significant hyperuricemia are relative contraindications.
Bezafibrate
Bezafibrate is a fibrate, and gout is not on the fibrate contraindication list. Niacin is the one to avoid.
